newsitem.title: UK: Disparities remain in China's consumer market.
newsitem.headline: Disparities remain in China's consumer market.

text.p: China is poised to become one of the world's top six trading nations by the year 2005, but even as the consumer market grows marked differences remain between urban and rural residents, according to a study released on Wednesday.

Only a small proportion of China's 1.6 billion population can afford Western-style consumer goods, electronics and processed foods, Euromonitor, a market research firm, reported in its study, Consumer China 1997.

In 1994 there were 86 colour televisions per 100 urban households, but only 17 colour televisions per 100 rural households. Similarly, there were 62 refrigerators per 100 urban households versus five in rural areas, 87 washing machines per 100 urban homes versus 17 in rural areas, 30 cameras per 100 urban homes versus 1.4 in rural homes, and 16 video recorders in urban homes versus one in rural area, Euromonitor said.

Bicycles remain the most popular vehicle in China, with 50 million bikes sold in 1995, up 50 percent from 1990, but still representing only 42 bikes per 1,000 people. Sales of motorbikes increased to 11 million in 1995 from 1.2 million in 1990, and car sales rose to 390,000 last year from 61,000 in 1990, Euromonitor reported.
Sales of audio systems increased about 85 percent to 3.2 billion in 1995 from 1.7 billion in 1990, and sales of laser disc players growing to 600,000 from 10,000 over the same period.

The Chinese each ate an average of 119 kilograms of vegetables in 1995, compared to 29 kilograms of meat and seven kilograms of seafood. Rice remains a dietary staple, with average consumption at 85 kilograms in 1995 versus nine kilograms of potatoes. By contrast, consumption of dairy products remains low. The Chinese each ate 3.22 grams of cheese in 1995, 3.22 grams of butter, 0.39 grams of ice cream and 0.37 grams of yoghurt, Euromonitor said.
Alcohol consumption is popular, with a total of 11 billion litres of beer consumed in 1995, 267 million litres of wine and seven billion litres of grain spirits, the study found.
